title: Landscape‐Scale Regulation of Sediment Nitrogen Cycling and N2O Production in Small Artificial Lakes Across an Urbanization Gradient
content:
Abstract

Small artificial lakes are ubiquitous in human-dominated landscapes, yet the responses of their sediment nitrogen (N) cycling and N2O production to land use change remain poorly constrained. We investigated sediment N pools, microbial biomass, transformation rates (nitrification, denitrification, nitritation, and ammonification) and N2O production potential across 54 small artificial lakes spanning an urbanization gradient of in Chongqing metropolitan, China. We further explored the effects of landscape composition across multiple spatial scales on N cycling in lake sediments. Results revealed that sediment N transformation rates and N2O production potential showed a consistent increase from forest to agricultural and urban landscapes. Watershed integrated land-use index within multi-scale buffer zones (50–2,000 m) exhibited significant positive correlations with N transformation rates and N2O production potential in sediments. This signifies intensified urban landscape substantially accelerate these processes by increasing N substrate abundance and bioavailability, as well as microbial biomass. These landscape controls are particularly scale-dependent, with nearshore land-use patterns within an ∼800 m buffer zone explaining the most spatial variability in N cycling rates and N2O production. Furthermore, landscape changes alter not only the magnitude but also the structure of sediment N cycling networks, resulting in imbalanced, disproportionately enhanced denitrification and N2O production potential in urbanized lakes. Our results demonstrate a landscape–sediment–microbe cascade governing N cycling and N2O generation in small artificial lakes, highlighting their role as heterogeneous biogeochemical reactors. Incorporating scale-dependent landscape controls and sediment processes is essential for improving N cycling modeling and prediction in rapidly urbanizing watersheds.
